claims.text: Equivalent thermomechanical processing yields single-phase FCC microstructures in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has more pronounced atomic-scale lattice distortion than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy has more pronounced short-range-order fluctuations than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Lattice distortion and short-range-order fluctuations act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Greater obstruction of dislocation motion in the quinary alloy enhances strain hardening.
Greater obstruction of dislocation motion in the quinary alloy delays strain localization.
The five-element alloy has a more heterogeneous bonding environment than its lower-order subsets.
A more heterogeneous bonding environment produces enhanced local lattice distortion.
Enhanced local lattice distortion impedes dislocation glide.
Enhanced local lattice distortion promotes dynamic recovery, cross-slip, and twinning.
Dynamic recovery, cross-slip, and twinning collectively contribute to a higher strain-hardening rate.
Reducing the number of constituents reduces lattice-distortion and short-range-order effects.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary subsets will have lower strain-hardening exponents.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary subsets will begin localized necking earlier.
Earlier necking in the quaternary and ternary subsets will result in lower tensile ductility.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit less overall work hardening than the quinary alloy.
The proposed relationships are limited to similarly processed, single-phase FCC alloys tested in uniaxial tension at room temperature and constant strain rate.
Grain size and residual stresses may affect the quantitative relationship between lattice distortion, short-range order, and strain hardening.
